item.text:
I did not score. I used the local prior only as grounding and then selected a tight ruler-specific source set for 2022.

**Office, Authority, Constraints**
- Kishida was Japan’s prime minister throughout 2022. His official profile page shows him as the 101st PM, and as a House of Representatives member from Hiroshima 1st District.
- Constitutionally, executive power sits with the Cabinet, the PM is designated by the Diet, and the PM appoints and can dismiss ministers. In practice, that means Kishida had real agenda-setting power but remained constrained by Diet confidence, the lower-house majority rule, and coalition management.
- The key 2022 practical constraints were: the LDP-Komeito coalition, the shock from Abe’s assassination, the Unification Church backlash, inflation/yen weakness, COVID spillovers, and the December 2022 security reset after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and rising regional tension.

**Retained Sources**
1. [内閣総理大臣　岸田　文雄](https://www.kantei.go.jp/jp/100_kishida/meibo/daijin/kishida_fumio.html) - Publisher: 首相官邸; Date: current profile page; Precise fact: Kishida is PM and a Hiroshima 1st District lower-house member with prior foreign and defense posts; Period fit: anchors his office in 2022; Ruler attribution: direct official biography; Limitations: self-presentation, not independent assessment; Contrary point: no evidence here of actual leverage or popularity.

2. [Diet-related Laws The Constitution of Japan](https://www.sangiin.go.jp/eng/law/tcoj/index.htm) - Publisher: House of Councillors; Date: current official text of the Constitution; Precise fact: Articles 65-68 make the Cabinet the executive authority, require PM designation by the Diet, and give the PM appointment/removal power over ministers; Period fit: defines the institutional constraints for all of 2022; Ruler attribution: legal framework, not Kishida-specific; Limitations: law on paper, not actual political bargaining; Contrary point: does not explain coalition politics or party faction pressures.

3. [Policy Speech by Prime Minister KISHIDA Fumio to the 208th Session of the Diet](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202201/_00009.html) - Publisher: Prime Minister’s Office of Japan; Date: January 17, 2022; Precise fact: Kishida framed COVID response, wage growth, “New Form of Capitalism,” and alliance security as core priorities; Period fit: establishes the opening 2022 agenda before the major shocks of the year; Ruler attribution: direct first-person agenda statement; Limitations: aspirational, not outcome evidence; Contrary point: policy declarations do not prove implementation success.

4. [Address by Prime Minister KISHIDA Fumio at the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Ceremony](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202408/06hiroshima.html) - Publisher: Prime Minister’s Office of Japan; Date: August 6, 2024, but it reflects the same Hiroshima-centered nuclear framing Kishida used in office; Precise fact: Kishida ties Japan’s postwar identity to the Three Non-Nuclear Principles and nuclear abolition; Period fit: useful for Chapter 1B’s nuclear/disarmament lens and Kishida’s Hiroshima-based identity; Ruler attribution: direct official speech; Limitations: later publication date than 2022, so use as background only if needed; Contrary point: it is normative rhetoric, not evidence of policy delivery in 2022.

5. [Japan's ruling coalition makes strong election showing after Abe killing](https://www.euronews.com/2022/07/10/us-japan-election) - Publisher: Reuters via Euronews; Date: July 10, 2022; Precise fact: Kishida’s LDP-Komeito coalition expanded its upper-house majority two days after Abe’s assassination; Period fit: captures the immediate political effect of the July shock; Ruler attribution: directly about Kishida’s government and coalition; Limitations: exit-poll and early-result reporting; Contrary point: a stronger seat position did not prevent later approval collapse.

6. [Japan PM shuffles cabinet as anger deepens over ties to Unification Church](https://www.euronews.com/2022/08/11/us-japan-politics) - Publisher: Reuters via Euronews; Date: August 11, 2022; Precise fact: Kishida reshuffled his cabinet amid public anger over LDP ties to the Unification Church and support deterioration; Period fit: explains the post-assassination political damage-control phase; Ruler attribution: explicitly Kishida’s cabinet move; Limitations: contemporaneous wire reporting, not final historical judgment; Contrary point: reshuffle addressed symptoms more than structural trust loss.

7. [令和４年８月３１日岸田内閣総理大臣記者会見終了後の書面による質問に対する回答](https://www.kantei.go.jp/jp/pages/20220831kaiken_shomen.html) - Publisher: 首相官邸; Date: August 31, 2022; Precise fact: the PMO answers questions on Unification Church ties, confirms government distance from the church, and discusses state-funeral attendance logistics; Period fit: shows the official damage-control line in the most sensitive period; Ruler attribution: direct governmental response from Kishida’s office; Limitations: defensive framing, no independent validation of party practices; Contrary point: carefully worded responses do not resolve the underlying trust problem.

8. [Japan Kishida's support hits low on his party's ties to controversial church](https://www.euronews.com/2022/10/10/japan-politics) - Publisher: Reuters via Euronews; Date: October 10, 2022; Precise fact: Kishida’s cabinet support fell to a one-year low as church-tie controversy and inflation pressures mounted; Period fit: strong evidence for the late-2022 political constraint environment; Ruler attribution: directly about Kishida’s cabinet; Limitations: polls are volatile and question-wording sensitive; Contrary point: low support does not by itself show policy incapacity.

9. [岸田首相「率直におわび」 自民党議員と旧統一教会の関係巡り](https://mainichi.jp/articles/20220831/k00/00m/010/248000c) - Publisher: Mainichi Shimbun; Date: August 31, 2022; Precise fact: Kishida publicly apologized over LDP lawmakers’ ties to the former Unification Church; Period fit: local-language critical coverage of the trust crisis; Ruler attribution: direct Kishida response in Japanese domestic press; Limitations: short news package, not a full investigation; Contrary point: apology is not proof of personal involvement.

10. [Japan PM Kishida's support tumbles, hit by questions over church and COVID](https://www.euronews.com/2022/08/22/us-japan-politics) - Publisher: Reuters via Euronews; Date: August 22, 2022; Precise fact: support dropped sharply as church ties and COVID management became major criticism points; Period fit: captures the immediate post-reshuffle backlash; Ruler attribution: directly tied to Kishida’s cabinet; Limitations: one poll cycle; Contrary point: it mixes church and pandemic issues, so it does not isolate causality.

11. [Kishida disapproval rate edges above 40% on church ties, Abe funeral](https://www.euronews.com/2022/09/05/japan-politics) - Publisher: Reuters via Euronews; Date: September 5, 2022; Precise fact: disapproval rose over the church issue and opposition to Abe’s state funeral; Period fit: connects the two biggest legitimacy controversies of late 2022; Ruler attribution: directly about Kishida’s cabinet; Limitations: polling snapshot, not a causal study; Contrary point: public opposition to the funeral was broader than criticism of Kishida alone.

12. [Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202212/_00006.html) - Publisher: Prime Minister’s Office of Japan; Date: December 16, 2022; Precise fact: Kishida announced the new National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy, and Defense Buildup Program, with a 43 trillion-yen buildup and 2% GDP target by FY2027; Period fit: the year-end security pivot that defines late-2022 governance; Ruler attribution: direct first-person decision announcement; Limitations: policy announcement, not implementation; Contrary point: the speech shows intent and process, not verified effectiveness.

**Compact Event Map**
- January 17: Kishida opens 2022 with COVID response, wage growth, and “New Form of Capitalism.”
- Spring 2022: Ukraine war and regional security deterioration push Japan toward a harder security line.
- July 8-10: Abe is assassinated; Kishida then wins a stronger upper-house position, but under the shadow of security lapses.
- August 10-31: cabinet reshuffle, then the Unification Church controversy becomes a dominant constraint.
- September 27: Abe’s state funeral becomes a legitimacy flashpoint.
- October: support hits new lows as church ties and inflation bite.
- December 16: Kishida formalizes the security reset with the three national security documents and a large defense buildup.
